before: == asks the class’s value-comparison rule; Array compares elements. equal? tests whether two references identify the very same object. Separate arrays can be value-equal without being identical.

Hash uses hash and eql? together to identify keys. Integer 1 and Float 1.0 compare equal with == but not with eql?, so they are distinct hash keys. A custom key type that overrides eql? must provide a consistent hash result for equal keys; do not mutate key identity fields while stored.

receiver.hash takes no explicit argument and returns an integer hash code. Objects that are eql? must produce equal hash codes; do not depend on a particular code remaining the same between processes. Here two equal arrays satisfy that rule.
```ruby
a = [1]
b = [1]
puts a.eql?(b)
puts a.hash == b.hash
```
It prints:
```text
true
true
```

This comparison asks about identity, not whether both arrays hold one.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
a = [1]
b = [1]
puts a == b
puts a.equal?(b)
puts 1 == 1.0
puts 1.eql?(1.0)
lookup = {1 => "integer"}
puts lookup.fetch(1.0, "missing")
```

The output is `true`, then `false`, then `true`, then `false`, then `missing`. The later hash lookup uses a stricter kind of key match than ordinary numeric equality: integer one and 1.0 are different keys here.
